title: Pressure on a surface
body: P = \frac{F_{\perp}}{A}
caution: Pressure is a scalar, so label force arrows with the force due to the pressure (F = PA), not with P. In a net-force equation write PA - P_{atm}A - Mg = 0, not bare pressures mixed with forces.
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.1.ii: "the ratio of the sum of the magnitudes of the perpendicular components of the forces exerted by the gas's atoms on the surface to the area of the surface"

title: Gas pressure (kinetic theory)
body: The pressure a gas exerts on a surface is the sum of the perpendicular force components from its atoms' collisions with the surface divided by the surface area, and pressure exists throughout the gas, not just at the boundary.
ced_evidence: 9.1.A.1.ii, 9.1.A.1.iii: "Pressure exists throughout the gas itself, not just at the boundary"

title: Average kinetic energy and rms speed
body: K_{avg} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT = \frac{1}{2}mv_{rms}^2
ced_evidence: 9.1.B.1.ii: "K avg = 3/2 kBT = 1/2 m vrms^2"

title: Temperature (atomic description)
body: The temperature of a system is characterized by the average kinetic energy of the atoms within that system.
ced_evidence: 9.1.B.1: "characterized by the average kinetic energy of the atoms within that system"

title: Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution (qualitative)
body: A graph of the energies or speeds of atoms at a given temperature; students relate its features to temperature but need not know its functional form.

items.label: Vertical axis
items.meaning: Relative number of atoms at each speed or energy

items.label: Curve features
items.meaning: Features of the curve are related to the gas temperature

ced_evidence: 9.1.B.1.i: "The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution provides a graphical representation of the energies and speeds of atoms at a given temperature."

title: Classical ideal gas model assumptions
body: The four assumptions of the classical model of an ideal gas.

items.meaning: Instantaneous velocities of atoms are random
Volumes of the atoms are negligible compared to the total volume occupied by the gas
The only appreciable forces on the atoms are those that occur during collisions

ced_evidence: 9.2.A.1: "instantaneous velocities of atoms are random, the volumes of the atoms are negligible..."

title: Ideal gas law
body: PV = nRT = Nk_BT
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.2: "PV = nRT = NkBT"

title: Zero-pressure temperature from a P–T graph
body: The temperature at which an ideal gas has zero pressure is found by extrapolating a graph of pressure as a function of temperature.
ced_evidence: 9.2.A.4: "extrapolated from a graph of pressure as a function of temperature"

title: Heating and cooling
body: Heating is the transfer of energy into a system by thermal processes, and cooling is the transfer of energy out of a system by thermal processes.

title: Thermal contact
body: Two systems are in thermal contact if they may transfer energy by thermal processes.
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.1: "Two systems are in thermal contact if..."

title: Thermal processes of energy transfer
body: The three thermal processes that transfer energy between systems at different temperatures.
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.2: "conduction, convection, and radiation"

title: Direction of spontaneous thermal transfer
body: Energy is transferred through thermal processes spontaneously from the higher-temperature system to the lower-temperature system, because in atomic collisions energy is most likely transferred from higher-energy to lower-energy atoms.
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.3: "spontaneously from a higher-temperature system to a lower-temperature system"

title: Thermal equilibrium
body: Thermal equilibrium results when no net energy is transferred by thermal processes between two systems in thermal contact; after many collisions the most probable state is one in which both systems have the same temperature.
ced_evidence: 9.3.A.4: "no net energy is transferred by thermal processes"; 9.3.A.3.ii

title: Internal energy
body: The internal energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic energy of the objects that make up the system and the potential energy of the configuration of those objects.
ced_evidence: 9.4.A.1: "sum of the kinetic energy of the objects that make up the system and the potential energy of the configuration"

title: Internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas
body: U = \frac{3}{2}nRT = \frac{3}{2}Nk_BT

title: Ideal gas has no internal potential energy
body: Atoms in an ideal gas do not interact via conservative forces and their internal structure is not considered, so an ideal gas has no internal potential energy and its internal energy is the sum of the atoms' kinetic energies.
ced_evidence: 9.4.A.1.i: "an ideal gas does not have internal potential energy"

title: First law of thermodynamics
body: \Delta U = Q + W
caution: Here W is the work done ON the system, and Q is energy transferred to the system by heating (negative for cooling).
ced_evidence: 9.4.B.1.ii: "the change in internal energy is the sum of energy transferred to or from the system by heating, or work done on the system"

title: Work done on a gas at constant pressure
body: W = -P\Delta V
caution: The sign matters: W is work done on the gas, so it is positive when the gas is compressed (\Delta V < 0) and negative when it expands. The PV-diagram area gives only the absolute value.
ced_evidence: 9.4.B.1.iii: "work done on a system by a constant or average external pressure that changes the volume"

title: Pressure–volume (PV) diagram
body: A graph of pressure versus volume used to represent thermodynamic processes.

items.label: Axes
items.meaning: Pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis

items.label: Isotherm
items.meaning: A line of constant temperature on the diagram

items.label: Area under the curve
items.meaning: Its absolute value equals the work done on the gas when it expands or compresses

ced_evidence: 9.4.B.2, 9.4.B.2.i, 9.4.B.2.ii: "equal to the area underneath the curve"

title: Special-case thermodynamic processes
body: The named special cases of thermal processes.

items.label: Adiabatic
items.meaning: No energy transferred to or from the system through thermal processes

ced_evidence: 9.4.B.3: "constant volume (isovolumetric), constant temperature (isothermal), and constant pressure (isobaric)... (adiabatic)"

title: Energy to change temperature (specific heat)
body: Q = mc\Delta T
ced_evidence: 9.5.A.1: "related to the material's specific heat"; boundary: specific heat modeled as independent of temperature

title: Rate of conductive energy transfer
body: \frac{Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{kA\Delta T}{L}
ced_evidence: 9.5.B.1: "related to the thermal conductivity, the physical dimensions of the material, and the temperature difference across the material"

title: Specific heat and thermal conductivity as intrinsic properties
body: Specific heat and thermal conductivity are intrinsic properties of a material that depend on the arrangement and interactions of its atoms.
ced_evidence: 9.5.A.2, 9.5.B.2: "intrinsic property of that material"

title: Second law of thermodynamics
body: The total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease and is constant only when all processes the system undergoes are reversible.
ced_evidence: 9.6.A.1: "total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease and is constant only when all processes... are reversible"

title: Entropy (qualitative)
body: Entropy is qualitatively the tendency of energy to spread, or the unavailability of some of the system's energy to do work.
ced_evidence: 9.6.A.2: "tendency of energy to spread or the unavailability of some of the system's energy to do work"

title: Entropy as a state function; maximum at equilibrium
body: Entropy depends only on the current state of a system, not how it got there, and is maximum when the system is in thermodynamic equilibrium.
ced_evidence: 9.6.A.2.ii, 9.6.A.2.iii: "Maximum entropy occurs when a system is in thermodynamic equilibrium"

title: Isolated vs. closed system entropy
body: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases, but the entropy of a closed system can decrease because energy can be transferred into or out of it.
ced_evidence: 9.6.A.3.ii: "the entropy of a closed system can decrease because energy can be transferred into or out of the system"
